followUps: I would code the concurrent hold and confirm first, because it is the hardest part and the one the interviewer will probe. Order for 45 minutes: 5 min scope, 5 min entities, then about 20 min on ShowSeat, the seat lock and hold/confirm, 10 min on a small driver that shows two users fighting for one seat, and the rest on extensions. Search, pricing and notifications can be stubbed behind interfaces and described aloud.

I would leave out real payments, search ranking, multiple cities and concerts, and distributed locking, and say so in the first minutes. They are big and add no new design idea inside 45 minutes. I keep a PaymentGateway interface with a fake, and mention Redis or database locks as an extension. Stating the cut list early shows judgement and stops the interviewer expecting it.

code.title: Same seat, different show: status lives on ShowSeat
code.python:
shows = ["09:00", "18:00", "22:00"]
# Status lives on (show, seat), not on the seat itself
show_seat = {(s, "B4"): "AVAILABLE" for s in shows}
show_seat[("18:00", "B4")] = "BOOKED"  # book B4 for the 6 pm show only
print("Seat B4 per show:")
for s in shows:
    print(s, show_seat[(s, "B4")])
# Rows per year: 5 shows a day * 365 days * 200 seats
print("rows per year per screen:", 5 * 365 * 200)

followUps: About 365,000 rows per screen per year, which is fine. With 5 shows a day, 365 days and 200 seats, that is 5 x 365 x 200 = 365,000. A theatre with 5 screens makes about 1.8 million, and a city with 100 screens 36 million. Rows are small and indexed by (show_id, seat_id), and old shows can be archived or partitioned by date, so storage is not the problem; hot rows are.

Eagerly at the moment a show is scheduled, in one batch. Then a seat always has a row, so the atomic update WHERE status='AVAILABLE' works and there is nothing to create under contention. Lazy creation (a missing row means available) saves space but turns booking into an insert race that needs a unique key. Eager creation also lets price per seat be fixed when the show is created.

code.title: Hold several seats atomically (check all, then take all)
code.python:
import threading

owner = {}                    # seat -> user
lock = threading.Lock()       # one lock per show

def hold(user, *seats):
    with lock:                # released automatically, even on error
        if any(s in owner for s in seats):   # check all first
            return False
        for s in seats:                      # then take all
            owner[s] = user
        return True

def show(b):
    return "true" if b else "false"

print("alice A1,A2 -> " + show(hold("alice", "A1", "A2")))
print("bob   A2,A3 -> " + show(hold("bob", "A2", "A3")))
print("bob   A3    -> " + show(hold("bob", "A3")))  # A3 was not leaked
print("owners: {" + ", ".join(k + "=" + v for k, v in sorted(owner.items())) + "}")

followUps: The hold may be lost without the server knowing: the lock or Redis key expires, another user takes the seat, then the paused server wakes up and still thinks it owns it. Protect against that with a fencing token: every hold gets an increasing number, and confirm checks that the token is still the latest. Also re-check status and expiry in the database at confirm, so the stale server fails safely instead of overwriting.

Pessimistic or a conditional atomic update, because a blockbuster release means many users fighting for the same few seats. Optimistic retries would mostly fail and waste work. The simplest version is one statement: UPDATE ... SET status='HELD' WHERE seat_id IN (...) AND status='AVAILABLE', then compare the row count with the seats asked. Optimistic is fine for quiet shows, where conflicts are rare.

If the seat was not taken by anyone else yet, a design choice is to allow a short grace period of a few seconds; if payment already went through, the booking becomes EXPIRED and the payment is refunded.

Use the same code path that frees a seat: when a hold expires (found by lazy check or by the sweeper), call a seatFreed hook that offers the seat to the first user in the waitlist through an Observer. Notifications go through an event queue so slow SMS or email never blocks the lock. The offer gets its own short hold, e.g. 5 minutes, and if unused, passes to the next waiter.

code.title: Late payment: re-check the hold before confirming
code.python:
holder = "alice"
hold_until = 10   # hold ends at minute 10

# Re-check under the lock that the hold is still ours and not expired
def confirm(user, now):
    if user == holder and now < hold_until:
        return "CONFIRMED"
    return "EXPIRED -> refund with the same idempotency key"

print("payment done at t=8:  " + confirm("alice", 8))
print("payment done at t=12: " + confirm("alice", 12))
holder = "bob"   # someone else now legitimately holds the seat
print("late and taken by bob: " + confirm("alice", 8))

followUps: An idempotency key is a unique id the client sends with a request, so the gateway can recognise a retry and return the first result instead of charging again. Example: key bk-1042-pay is sent twice because of a timeout; the gateway charges once (Rs 500) and answers the second call with the stored result. The refund uses the same key family, so retries cannot refund twice. The gateway stores key and result for some days.

You can, but it is risky. Confirming first (marking seats BOOKED) and charging after means a failed payment must undo a booking and the seat may have been shown as sold to others. The usual safe order is hold, charge, confirm, because a hold is cheap to release. Confirm-first works only where unpaid bookings are allowed, such as pay-at-venue, with a payment deadline and automatic cancel.

Store each amount with its currency, e.g. paise plus code INR, and keep balances per currency pair rather than adding different currencies. Convert only when settling or displaying, using an exchange rate stored with the expense, so history never changes when rates move. Example: Rs 8,300 at 83 per dollar is stored as 100 USD plus the rate 83. Balances are then a map from (pair, currency) to amount.

Because expenses are immutable and are the source of truth, throw the balance sheet away and replay every expense in order, applying each split with sign +1, and each edit or delete as the reverse entry. This is O(number of expenses). Then compare with the old balances and check that the sum of all net balances is exactly 0. Keep this as an admin job and run it nightly as a consistency check.

code.title: Money in integer paise: exact 3-way split
code.python:
# Split total paise among n people; the first (total % n) people get one extra paisa
def split(total, n):
    return [total // n + (1 if i < total % n else 0) for i in range(n)]

def b(x):
    return "true" if x else "false"

a, c = 0.1, 0.2
print("double: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 -> " + b(a + c == 0.3))
x, y = 10, 20   # the same amounts in paise
print("paise:  10 + 20 == 30 -> " + b(x + y == 30))
p = split(10000, 3)   # Rs 100.00 in three parts
print("split 10000 paise in 3: [" + ", ".join(map(str, p)) + "] sum=" + str(sum(p)))

followUps: Work in paise: 10000 paise divided by 3 is 3333 remainder 1, so the shares are 3334, 3333 and 3333, which add to exactly 10000. Give the leftover paisa to the first person, or to the payer or by a fixed rule so it is deterministic. For ratio 1:2:3 on 10000: floors 1666, 3333, 5000 total 9999, so 1 paisa remains; give it to the largest fractional part. The parts always add up to the total.

Use a decimal type when amounts need many digits after the point or non-standard scales, such as interest rates, tax percentages, fuel prices per litre, or currencies with 3 decimals (the dinar). It is also easier when you apply percentages to money. Still set an explicit scale and rounding mode, build it from strings, and round to minor units once at the end. For plain add and subtract of rupees, integer paise is simpler and faster.

code.title: Greedy debt simplification on net balances
code.python:
names = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
net = [-40, -15, 30, 25]   # net balance per person; negative = owes; sum = 0
print("net: A=-40 B=-15 C=30 D=25")
while True:
    d = net.index(min(net))   # biggest debtor
    c = net.index(max(net))   # biggest creditor
    if net[d] == 0:
        break
    pay = min(-net[d], net[c])   # this step zeroes at least one person
    print(names[d] + " pays " + names[c] + " " + str(pay))
    net[d] += pay
    net[c] -= pay

followUps: Take nets A=-3, B=-2, C=-4, D=+5, E=+4 (sum 0). Greedy: C pays D 4, A pays E 3... then B pays D 1, B pays E 1, total 4 transfers. Optimum: the group {A=-3,B=-2,D=+5} nets to 0 and {C=-4,E=+4} nets to 0, so A pays D 3, B pays D 2, C pays E 4, only 3 transfers. Best is n minus the number of zero-sum groups, here 5 - 2 = 3.

Only allow payments along existing pairs of people who already owe each other (edges of the debt graph). Then the problem becomes a flow problem: cancel cycles first (A owes B, B owes C, C owes A) and push money along existing edges, which can be done with a max-flow or cycle cancelling method. You may not reach the minimum number of transfers, but nobody pays a stranger. Offer it as a group setting.

Example: Rs 600 of items, Rs 60 tax; a person with Rs 150 of items gets 150/600 x 60 = Rs 15 of tax. If the shares do not add up to the bill by 1 or 2 paise, hand out the extra paise one at a time to the largest fractions. Finally assert that the sum equals the total.

Use one Expense request with a type field and a type-specific payload, e.g. {type: "ITEMS", items: [{price, sharedBy: [A,B]}], tax, tip}. The service looks up the strategy by type in the registry, and the strategy validates its own payload. The API stays stable as new types arrive; only the payload shape changes. Reject unknown types with a clear error.

Check all books first, then change anything, and do the changes inside one transaction or under locks taken in a fixed order (member, then copies sorted by id). If any book fails a rule or any update fails, roll back everything and report the reason. In memory, collect the copies, verify all, then mark all LOANED. In a database, wrap it in a transaction so either all loans exist or none do.

Compute the due date with a Calendar or holiday service: add loan days, then if the date falls on a closed day, move to the next open day. Example: a 14-day loan from 1 June due 15 June, a holiday, becomes 16 June. Keep holidays in data, not code, so the library can change them. Fines then skip closed days too, so a member is never fined for a day the library was shut.

code.title: FIFO reservation queue when a copy is freed
code.python:
from collections import deque

queue = deque(["bob", "cara"])   # FIFO waiters for this title

# Called whenever a copy is returned or a hold expires
def copy_freed(today):
    if not queue:
        print("day %d: copy AVAILABLE" % today)
        return
    nxt = queue.popleft()
    print("day %d: copy ON_HOLD for %s until day %d" % (today, nxt, today + 3))

copy_freed(10)   # book returned: first waiter gets it
copy_freed(13)   # bob's hold expired: the same path serves the next waiter
copy_freed(16)   # cara's hold expired: nobody left

followUps: Skip them and move on to the next waiter, but do it by rule, not by hand: the hold check can include the lending rules, and a blocked member keeps their place or is moved, depending on policy. Notify them that the hold is blocked by fines. The copy never sits idle: if nobody eligible is waiting, it goes to AVAILABLE. Document the policy so it is predictable.

Yes. Each returned copy of the same title triggers copyFreed separately, so two copies serve the first two waiters, each with its own hold. Example: queue bob, cara, dan and two returns on the same day: bob and cara each get a copy ON_HOLD, dan stays waiting. Because the queue is per title and not per copy, nobody can be skipped by accident.

followUps:
Count only open days. Take the list of holidays, walk from due date to return date and count the days that are not holidays or closed days. Example: due Monday, returned the next Monday, with Sunday closed: 7 calendar days, 6 fine days. Sketch:

int late = 0;
for (d = due + 1; d <= returned; d++)
  if (!calendar.isClosed(d)) late++;

For long periods, use prefix counts of open days to answer in O(1).

Only staff with a waiver permission, such as a librarian lead, and every waiver is a new ledger entry, not an edit. The entry holds who, when, how much and a reason, for example: charged Rs 29 on day 10, waived Rs 29 by staff-17 for a documented illness. The fine balance is the sum of entries, so history is never lost and an audit can replay it. Large waivers can require a second approval.

Drop Observer, Decorator and Chain of Responsibility first, and keep Strategy, a state enum with a transition check, and interfaces for the lock and the payment gateway. Those give the most value for the least code and let you explain extension points aloud. Notifications can be a single method call to a stub, and stacked price rules can be an if. Add the dropped patterns later only if time remains.

Over-engineering costs time you need for the hard part, and unfinished code scores worse than simple code. Signs: an interface with one implementation and no real variation, factories for objects built once, deep class hierarchies, and generic frameworks for rules that are three ifs. Pattern for a reason only: add a pattern when a requirement varies or when you must test with a fake. Working code first, then refactor.

Stress tests pass by luck because the thread schedule varies and the race window may be only a few instructions. A racy increment can survive millions of runs on a fast machine with few cores. To raise the chance of failure, use a start gate, many more threads than cores, many rounds, and small random sleeps or yields in critical sections. Passing is never a proof, which is why you also reason about invariants and use tools like jcstress or ThreadSanitizer.

Run the real service against a real Redis (for example in a container) with several app instances or many client threads hitting overlapping seats, then check invariants in the database afterwards. Add fault tests: kill a client after it takes a hold, delay it past the TTL, and restart Redis, and verify that fencing tokens reject stale confirms. Also test the Lua script on its own with fixed inputs, and use a fake clock only for the application logic.

A fencing token is a number that grows with every lock grant, and the protected resource rejects any write carrying an older number. A lock alone is not enough because a client can pause (GC, network), the lock expires, a second client gets the lock with token 34, and then the first wakes up believing it still holds token 33. The database sees 33 is older than 34 and refuses the write, so the stale client cannot corrupt data.

Use a coordinator (ZooKeeper, etcd, or a database lease table) that knows which node owns which show. When a node's lease expires, the coordinator reassigns its shows, and the new owner reloads state from the database, where confirmed bookings are durable. Holds in memory may be lost, so either accept that users retry, or store holds with expiry in the database. Use fencing on the ownership epoch so the old node cannot write after losing the lease.
